rows.recommendation: In apparently healthy people <70 years of age without established ASCVD, DM, CKD, genetic/rarer lipid or BP disorders, estimation of 10-year fatal and nonfatal CVD risk with SCORE2 is recommended.
In apparently healthy people ≥70 years of age without established ASCVD, DM, CKD, genetic/rarer lipid or BP disorder, estimation of 10-year fatal and nonfatal CVD risk with SCORE2-OP is recommended.
Patients with established ASCVD and/or DM and/or moderate-to-severe renal disease and/or genetic/rarer lipid or BP disorders are to be considered at high or very high CVD risk.

A stepwise treatment-intensification approach aiming at intensive risk factor treatment is recommended for apparently healthy people at high or very high ASCVD risk, as well as patients with established ASCVD and/or DM, with consideration of CVD risk, treatment benefit of risk factors, risk modifiers, comorbidities, and patient preferences.

Treatment of ASCVD risk factors is recommended in apparently healthy people without DM, CKD, genetic/rarer lipid or BP disorders who are at very high CVD risk (SCORE2 ≥7.5% for age under 50; SCORE2 ≥10% for age 50–69; SCORE2-OP ≥15% for age ≥70).
An informed discussion about CVD risk and treatment benefits tailored to the needs of a patient is recommended.
It is recommended that mental disorders with either significant functional impairment or decreased use of healthcare systems be considered as influencing

Treatment of ASCVD risk factors should be considered in apparently healthy people without DM, CKD, genetic/rarer lipid, or BP disorders who are at high CVD risk (SCORE2 2.5 to <7.5% for age under 50; SCORE2 5 to <10% for age 50–69; SCORE2-OP 7.5 to <15% for age ≥70 years), taking ASCVD risk modifiers, lifetime risk and treatment benefit, and patient preferences into account.

In apparently healthy people, after estimation of 10-year fatal and non-fatal CVD risk, lifetime risk and treatment benefit, risk modifiers, frailty, polypharmacy, and patient preferences should be considered.
Presence of migraine with aura should be considered in CVD risk assessment.
Assessment of CVD risk should be considered in men with ED.
In women with a history of premature or stillbirth, periodic screening for hypertension and DM may be considered.
Assessment of total CVD risk may be considered in adults with chronic inflammatory conditions.
Avoidance of combined hormonal contraceptives may be considered in women with migraine with aura.
It is recommended to reduce sedentary time to engage in at least light activity throughout the day to reduce all-cause and CV mortality and morbidity.

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to adopt a Mediterranean or similar diet to lower risk of CVD.
It is recommended to restrict alcohol consumption to a maximum of 100 g per week.

Patients with mental disorders need intensified attention and support to improve adherence to lifestyle changes and drug treatment.
Smoking cessation is recommended regardless of weight gain, as weight gain does not lessen the ASCVD benefits of cessation.
In patients with established ASCVD, lipid-lowering treatment with an ultimate LDL-C goal of <1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and a ≥50% reduction of LDL-C vs. baseline is recommended.
For secondary prevention patients not achieving their goals on a maximum tolerated dose of a statin and ezetimibe, combination therapy including a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended.

In patients with type 2 DM at very high risk (e.g. with established ASCVD and/or severe TOD), intensive lipid-lowering therapy, ultimately aiming at ≥50% LDL-C reduction and an LDL-C of <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) is recommended.
In patients with type 2 DM >40 years of age at high risk, lipid-lowering treatment with an ultimate LDL-C goal of ≥50% LDL-C reduction and an LDL-C of <1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) is recommended.
It is recommended that the first objective of treatment is to lower BP to <140/90 mmHg in all patients, and that subsequent BP targets are tailored to age and specific comorbidities.
In treated patients aged 18–69 years, it is recommended that SBP should ultimately be lowered to a target range of 120–130 mmHg in most patients.
In treated patients aged ≥70 years, it is recommended that SBP should generally be targeted to <140 and down to 130 mmHg if tolerated.
In all treated patients, DBP is recommended to be lowered to <80 mmHg.
In persons with type 2 DM and ASCVD, the use of a GLP-1RA or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven outcome benefits is recommended to reduce CV and/or cardiorenal outcomes.
In patients with type 2 DM and CKD, the use of an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended to improve CVD and/or cardiorenal outcomes.
In patients with type 2 DM and HFrEF, use of an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven outcome benefits is recommended to lessen HF hospitalizations and CV death.

Participation in a medically supervised, structured, comprehensive, multidisciplinary EBCR and prevention programme for patients after ASCVD events and/or revascularization, and for patients with HF (mainly HFrEF), is recommended to improve patient outcomes.

section_headings: 3.2.3.3 Translating cardiovascular disease risk to treatment thresholds
content.narrative_summary: The text continues discussion of the SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP algorithms for estimating 5- and 10-year fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk adjusted for competing non-CVD mortality in healthy individuals aged ≥70 years. SCORE2/SCORE2-OP are calibrated into four clusters of countries (low, moderate, high, and very high risk) based on WHO national CVD mortality data, with specific country lists provided for each risk category. SCORE2 charts are freely available but exclude persons with pre-existing CVD or certain high-risk conditions, and pregnant women. To estimate an individual’s 10-year risk, one selects the country cluster, sex, smoking status, and age to find the nearest cell for BP and non-HDL-C, then adjusts the risk upward if the person’s BP or non-HDL-C approaches the next age category.

content.narrative_summary: The text describes age-specific 10-year CVD risk thresholds using SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP, highlighting that risk categories (low-to-moderate, high, very high) have numerically higher cut-offs in older age groups to prevent undertreatment in the young and overtreatment in the elderly. It emphasizes that risk categories do not automatically dictate treatment decisions, which should consider modifiers, lifetime risk, comorbidities, frailty, and patient preference. Lifestyle change (e.g., smoking cessation) can lower category without drugs. In persons ≥70 years, primary prevention with lipid-lowering is a Class IIb recommendation. In those 50–69 years, a 5% mortality risk threshold with the old SCORE corresponds to a 10% composite risk with SCORE2, identifying similar numbers for treatment qualification.

3.2.3.5 Risk estimation and risk factor treatment estimation in apparently healthy people ≥70 years of age
content.narrative_summary: The text discusses how 10-year CVD risk thresholds guide treatment decisions and resource allocation. A 10-year CVD risk ≥10% is considered ‘very high risk’ and warrants treatment of risk factors; a risk of 5–<10% is ‘high risk’ and also merits intervention. For people aged 50–69 years, stopping smoking, lifestyle modifications, and SBP <160 mmHg are recommended. Risk modifiers (e.g., in low-/moderate-risk regions, new risk factor thresholds) and patient preferences should be considered. For those ≥70 years, similar lifestyle and blood pressure targets apply, with age as the dominant driver of CVD risk.

3.2.3.7 Risk estimation and risk factor treatment in patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
content.narrative_summary: This page discusses lifetime CVD risk thresholds and recommended treatment approaches across age groups. For individuals ≥70 years, a 10-year CVD risk >15% is ‘very high risk’ and risk-factor treatment is recommended; a risk of 7.5–15% is ‘high risk’; and <7.5% is ‘low-to-moderate risk.’ Section 3.2.3.6 recommends, in apparently healthy people <50 years, quitting smoking, lifestyle changes, and maintaining SBP <160 mmHg; a 10-year CVD risk ≥7.5% is ‘very high risk,’ and risk factors should be treated. Section 3.2.3.7 outlines that patients with established ASCVD are at high risk of recurrent events and should receive smoking cessation, healthy lifestyle, and risk-factor treatment (STEP 1), with further intensification (STEP 2) as needed, considering 10-year risk, comorbidities, lifetime risk, treatment benefit, frailty, polypharmacy, and patient preferences.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Box 1
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Lifetime CVD risk and treatment benefit estimation
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Describes estimation of lifetime CVD risk and numerical lifetime benefit. Lifetime risk is the age at which there is a 50% probability of CVD event or death; lifetime benefit is the difference between predicted ages with and without treatment. Methods include clinical criteria (age, risk‐factor levels, modifiers), combining lifetime risk models with hazard ratios from RCTs, meta-analyses, Mendelian randomization, and online calculators. content.title: Figure 8. Flow chart of cardiovascular risk and risk factor treatment in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus
content.narrative_summary: This figure presents a stepwise flow chart for management of cardiovascular risk factors in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus according to ESC Guidelines. STEP 1 emphasizes smoking cessation, lifestyle modifications (Class I), and achieving HbA1c <53 mmol/mol (<7.0%, Class I), followed by risk stratification (absence or presence of established ASCVD or severe TOD). For patients without ASCVD/TOD, moderate or high risk determines blood pressure (SBP <140 to 130 mmHg, Class I) and LDL-C targets (<2.6 mmol/L, Class I or ≥50% reduction and <1.8 mmol/L, Class I) or de-escalation of prevention goals (Class III). Patients with ASCVD/TOD receive SBP and LDL-C targets, antithrombotic therapy (Class I), and addition of SGLT2-inhibitor or GLP-1 RA (Class I for CVD prevention, Class IIb for TOD). STEP 2 outlines intensified treatment based on 10-year or residual CVD risk, lifetime risk and benefit, comorbidities, frailty, and patient preferences, with SBP and LDL-C targets (Class I), SGLT2-i or GLP-1 RA if not already on it, and consideration of DAPT, DPI, or novel interventions (Class IIb).

content.narrative_summary: Dietary habits influence cardiovascular risk via effects on lipids, blood pressure, body weight and diabetes. content.narrative_summary: Secondary causes of dyslipidaemia (e.g. hypothyroidism, alcohol abuse, diabetes, Cushing’s syndrome, liver or kidney disease, certain drugs) should be excluded before lipid-lowering treatment. content.narrative_summary: The page discusses: (1) Statins as first-line therapy to reduce LDL-C and ASCVD risk, their effects on triglycerides, pancreatitis risk, and the need for coronary interventions; (2) Adverse effects of statins, notably myopathy, slight increases in blood glucose and HbA1c, rare rhabdomyolysis, and recommendations for managing myalgia without routine liver enzyme monitoring; (3) Ezetimibe adds LDL-C lowering benefit to statins, supported by meta-analyses and genetic studies, and is recommended second-line when statin therapy alone does not achieve goals; (4) PCSK9 inhibitors significantly reduce LDL-C (46–73% greater than placebo, ~30% more than ezetimibe), lower triglycerides, and apolipoproteins, with cost-effectiveness and long-term safety considerations pending; (5) Strategies for controlling plasma triglycerides include lifestyle measures and pharmacological agents (statins, fibrates, PCSK9 inhibitors, n-3 PUFAs); (6) Fibrates are used primarily for triglyceride lowering, with limited CVD outcome evidence and not routinely recommended in cardiovascular prevention, and guidelines for preventing pancreatitis when triglycerides are very high.

rows.recommendation: For secondary prevention patients not achieving their goals on a maximum tolerated dose of a statin and ezetimibe, combination therapy including a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended.

For very-high-risk FH patients (that is, with ASCVD or with another major risk factor) who do not achieve their goals on a maximum tolerated dose of a statin and ezetimibe, combination therapy including a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended.

If a statin-based regimen is not tolerated at any dosage (even after rechallenge), a PCSK9 inhibitor added to ezetimibe may be considered.
If the goal is not achieved, statin combination with a bile acid sequestrant may be considered.
Statin therapy is not recommended in premenopausal female patients who are considering pregnancy or are not using adequate contraception.

section_headings: Summary of recommendations for the clinical management of hypertension
Management of CVD risk in hypertensive patients
content.narrative_summary: The lower right prose notes that hypertension affects over 1 billion people worldwide (30–45% of adults, >60% of those aged >60 years), causes ~10 million deaths per year, and that despite evidence for BP-lowering treatments, detection, treatment, and control remain suboptimal. It also states that these recommendations apply to routine primary and secondary care and refers to the 2018 ESH Guidelines for complex cases.

recommendation_tables.title: Summary of recommendations for the clinical management of hypertension

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that BP should be classified as optimal, normal, high-normal, or grades 1 – 3 hypertension, according to office BP.
Repeated office BP measurements, on more than one visit, except when hypertension is severe (e.g. grade 3 and especially in high-risk patients).
Out-of-office BP measurement with ABPM and/or HBPM when feasible.

To evaluate for the presence of HMOD, measurement of serum creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes, and ACR is recommended for all patients. A 12-lead ECG is recommended for all patients, and echocardiography is recommended for those with ECG abnormalities or signs/symptoms of LV dysfunction. Fundoscopy or retinal imaging is recommended for patients with grades 2 or 3 hypertension and all hypertensive patients with DM.
For grade 1 hypertension, treatment initiation based on absolute CVD risk, estimated lifetime benefit, and the presence of HMOD is recommended.
For patients with grade 2 hypertension or higher, drug treatment is recommended.
It is recommended that the first objective of treatment is to lower BP to <140/90 mmHg in all patients, and that subsequent BP targets are tailored to age and specific comorbidities.
In treated patients aged 18–69 years, it is recommended that SBP should ultimately be lowered to a target range of 120 – 130 mmHg in most patients.
In treated patients aged ≥70 years, it is recommended that SBP should generally be targeted to <140 mmHg and down to 130 mmHg if tolerated.
In all treated patients, DBP is recommended to be lowered to <80 mmHg.
Lifestyle interventions are recommended for people with high-normal BP or higher.

recommendation_tables.title: Treatment of hypertension: drug treatment

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to initiate antihypertensive treatment with a two-drug combination in most patients, preferably as a single-pill combination. Exceptions are frail older patients and those with low-risk, grade 1 hypertension (particularly if SBP <150 mmHg).

It is recommended that the preferred combinations include a RAS blocker (i.e. an ACE inhibitor or ARB) with a CCB or diuretic, but other combinations of the five major classes can be used (ACE inhibitor, ARB, beta-blocker, CCB, thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic).

It is recommended, if BP remains uncontrolled with a two-drug combination, that treatment be increased to a three-drug combination, usually a RAS blocker with a CCB and a diuretic, preferably as a single-pill combination.

It is recommended, if BP is not controlled by a three-drug combination, that treatment should be increased by the addition of spironolactone, or if not tolerated, other diuretics such as amiloride or higher doses of other diuretics, an alpha-blocker or beta-blocker, or clonidine.
The combination of two RAS blockers is not recommended.

rows.recommendation: Statin therapy is recommended for many patients with hypertension.
Antiplatelet therapy is indicated for secondary prevention in patients with hypertension.

content.narrative_summary: This section describes the principles of ASCVD prevention in people with diabetes, emphasizing that beyond glucose management, blood pressure and LDL-C targets remain key. section_headings: 5. Policy interventions at the population level
content.narrative_summary: Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is described as a comprehensive, supervised, multidisciplinary intervention that includes exercise training, counselling, risk-factor modification, diet/nutritional counselling, vocational and psychosocial support. CR after ASCVD events or revascularization reduces hospitalizations, myocardial infarction, CV mortality, all-cause mortality, and depressive/anxiety symptoms. In patients with chronic heart failure (mainly HFrEF), exercise‐based CR improves mortality, reduces hospital admissions, and enhances exercise capacity and quality of life. CR is cost-effective. Key components include early initiation post-CV event, adequate supervision by trained professionals, individualized aerobic and muscular resistance exercise prescriptions based on pre-exercise screening, and sufficient dose (≥1000 minutes total exercise; ≥36 sessions). All recognized CV risk factors must be addressed during CR.

content.narrative_summary: Interventions for cerebrovascular diseases depend on the type of event (ischaemic or haemorrhagic). Ischaemic events are mainly caused by atherothrombosis, cardiac embolism, or small vessel disease; haemorrhagic events are due to hypertensive angiopathy or cerebral amyloid angiopathy, with bleeding precipitated by high blood pressure, anticoagulants, or coagulopathy. In ischaemic stroke or TIA, antithrombotics prevent further vascular events: cardioembolic stroke in AF requires anticoagulation, whereas in non-cardioembolic stroke antiplatelet agents (aspirin 75–150 mg/day, clopidogrel) are recommended. Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel or ticagrelor) is beneficial after minor ischaemic stroke or TIA, reducing recurrence at the cost of increased bleeding. Oral vitamin K antagonists offer no benefit over aspirin in non-cardioembolic stroke and carry higher bleeding risk.

In apparently healthy people ≥70 years of age without established ASCVD, DM, CKD, genetic/rarer lipid or BP disorder, estimation of 10-year fatal and nonfatal CVD risk with SCORE2-OP is recommended.
Patients with established CVD and/or DM and/or moderate-to-severe renal disease and/or genetic/rarer lipid or BP disorders are to be considered at high or very high CVD risk.

A stepwise treatment-intensification approach aiming at intensive risk factor treatment is recommended for apparently healthy people at high or very high CVD risk, as well as patients with established ASCVD and/or DM, with consideration of CVD risk, treatment benefit of risk factors, risk modifiers, comorbidities, and patient preferences.

An informed discussion about CVD risk and treatment benefits tailored to the needs of a patient is recommended.

The routine collection of other potential modifiers, such as genetic risk scores, circulating or urinary biomarkers, or vascular tests or imaging methods (other than CAC scoring or carotid ultrasound for plaque determination), is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for patients with cerebrovascular disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with a cerebrovascular event, improvement of lifestyle factors in addition to appropriate pharmacological management is recommended.

In patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA, prevention with antithrombotics is recommended; choice of antithrombotic depends on the mechanism of event. Use of an antiplatelet is recommended for patients with non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or TIA, and use of an anticoagulant is recommended in patients with cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or TIA.
In patients with non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or TIA, prevention with aspirin only, or dipyridamole plus aspirin, or clopidogrel alone is recommended.
In patients with stroke or TIA who have BP of 140/90 mmHg or higher, BP lowering is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for patients with lower extremity artery disease: best medical therapy

rows.recommendation: Smoking cessation is recommended in all patients with LEAD.
Healthy diet and PA are recommended for all patients with LEAD.
Supervised exercise training is recommended.
Non-supervised exercise training is recommended when supervised exercise training is not feasible or available.
Antiplatelet therapy is recommended in patients with symptomatic LEAD.
In patients with LEAD and hypertension, it is recommended to control BP at <140/90 mmHg.
In patients with LEAD and DM, strict glycaemic control is recommended.

content.narrative_summary: Quality indicators (QIs) are described as tools to evaluate care quality, enhance adherence to guideline recommendations, and benchmark provider performance. The ESC has published methodologies and disease‐specific QIs for cardiovascular conditions, integrated into practice and research programmes, although a comprehensive set for CVD prevention is still under development. Supplementary data—including additional figures, tables, and text—are available on the European Heart Journal and ESC websites.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations in patients with chronic kidney disease: best medical therapy

rows.recommendation: Treatment with an ACE inhibitor or an ARB is recommended in patients with DM, hypertension, and albuminuria. These medications should be titrated to the highest approved dose that is tolerated.
Combination treatment with ACE inhibitors and ARBs is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for lifestyle interventions and management of risk factors and concomitant diseases in patients with atrial fibrillation

rows.recommendation: Identification and management of risk factors and concomitant diseases are recommended to be considered an integral part of treatment.
Modification of unhealthy lifestyle and targeted therapy of intercurrent conditions is recommended to reduce AF burden and symptom severity.
Attention to good BP control is recommended in AF patients with hypertension to reduce AF recurrences and risk of stroke and bleeding.
